Somatic Symptom and Related Disorders

somatic symptom disorder · illness anxiety · functional neurological symptom disorder · factitious disorder · malingeringIs the symptom felt, feared or made on purpose, and if made, is there an external reward?

1Script2Urgent3Differential4Workup5Criteria6Severity7Treatment8Follow-upPractice
1Illness script
Bottom line
  • Distressing symptom outsized thoughts, worry or time somatic symptom disorder; typically over 6 months; real disease can coexist
  • Illness feared, with little or nothing felt illness anxiety (hypochondriasis), 6 months or more; motor or sensory change that fits no recognized neurologic disease, not on purpose functional neurological symptom disorder (conversion disorder); made on purpose factitious (no obvious reward) or malingering (external reward)
  • Scheduled brief visits limit testing CBT (cognitive behavioral therapy); an SSRI or SNRI (selective serotonin or serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor) may also help
What it is

1 or more symptoms that distress or disrupt daily life an outsized response to them

Symptomatic state lasts, typically over 6 months, even if no single symptom is constant

Driver

The response, not the symptom: thoughts, anxiety or time out of proportion

Symptoms may or may not have a medical explanation

Chain

Distressing symptom outsized worry and time more health care use, many clinicians

Unneeded testing more symptom-focused care

Outcome: more disability, iatrogenic harm and suicidality

Insights

A medical diagnosis does not exclude somatic symptom disorder: judge the response, not whether the symptom is explained

Deception separates factitious disorder and malingering from somatic symptom disorder; then the reward separates those two

The related disorders, side by sidesymptom, intent and reward
Somatic symptom1 or more distressing symptoms; excess thoughts, anxiety or timenot deceiving
Illness anxietyPreoccupied with having or getting a serious illness; symptoms absent or mildchecks the body again and again, or avoids care
Functional neurologicalAltered voluntary movement or sensationfindings do not fit recognized neurologic disease
FactitiousFalsifies or induces illness, in self or in someone else (typically a child, a dependent adult or a pet)deception even with no obvious external reward
MalingeringFakes or greatly exaggerates symptomsfor an external incentive
2Urgent risks
SuicideSomatic symptom disorder carries higher rates of suicidality and disability
TestingIatrogenic harm from tests and procedures that are not needed

If the workup for the same concern is already negative, choose limiting further evaluation.

Coexisting diseaseThe diagnosis does not rule out a concurrent medical condition
Symptoms may or may not be medically explained

If symptoms change significantly, or a new symptom or objective sign appears, choose examining and testing as in any patient.

Another personA caregiver falsifies or induces illness in a child, dependent adult or pet
Factitious disorder imposed on another; no obvious external reward

If a caregiver is suspected of falsifying or inducing a child's illness, even with no injury yet, choose reporting the suspicion to child protective services (adult protective services for a dependent adult).

3Differential
Look-alikes, most tempting first
DiagnosisFingerprintDecides it
Somatic symptom disorderDistressing symptom with outsized worry and time spent on itTypically over 6 months; a distressing symptom is present; not deceiving
Illness anxiety disorder (hypochondriasis)Fear of having or getting a serious illness; body checking or avoiding care6 months or more; symptoms absent or only mild
Functional neurological symptom disorder (conversion disorder)Change in voluntary movement or sensation, such as weakness, often after an acute stressorFindings incompatible with recognized neurologic disease (Hoover sign); not produced on purpose
Factitious disorder (Munchausen syndrome)Falsified or self-induced illnessDeception about one's own illness; no obvious external reward
MalingeringFaked or exaggerated symptomsAn external incentive
Factitious disorder imposed on another (Munchausen syndrome by proxy)A caregiver falsifies or induces illness in a dependentThe caregiver deceives; no obvious external reward
Belief about appearanceA fixed belief that a body part looks defective or ugly is body dysmorphic disorder, whose insight can be absent (delusional beliefs)A false belief about a bodily function1 month or more; fixed belief about a bodily function (an odor, a parasite) that clear evidence does not change
Recurrent unexpected attacks1 month or more of worry about more attacks or a behavior change; fear typically acute and episodic
Pain or difficulty with attempted vaginal penetration6 months or more; no wider preoccupation or repeated care seeking
First exclude a medical cause:
4Workup

A real disease does not rule out somatic symptom disorder, and somatic symptom disorder does not rule out a real disease.

Clues that change the answer
CluePoints toWhy
Distressing symptom; hours a day on it; many clinicians for the same concernSomatic symptom disorderThe response to a real, distressing symptom is out of proportion
Fears a serious disease; no or mild symptoms; checks the body oftenIllness anxiety disorderThe fear, not a symptom, is the problem
Heel of the weak leg presses down as the other leg lifts against resistanceFunctional neurological symptom disorderFindings incompatible with recognized neurologic disease (Hoover sign); not produced on purpose
Episodes, often with eyes forced shut, asynchronous movements and no confusion afterwardPsychogenic nonepileptic seizures (functional neurological symptom disorder)Video EEG of an event shows no epileptiform activity
Medical job or knowledge; self-induced wound; accepts invasive procedures; usually cooperative; no claim or lawsuitFactitious disorderDeception with no obvious external reward, so not malingering
External gain at stake; usually uncooperative; complaints stop once the gain is obtainedMalingeringDeception to obtain an external incentive

Pause point. The bait: one more scan or specialist referral after the workup for the same concern is already negative, or malingering offered when no external reward exists. Further testing can feed the cycle; deception with no obvious reward is factitious disorder.

5Diagnostic criteria
Defining criteria: somatic symptom disorder Symptom – 1 or more that distress or disrupt daily life · Response – thoughts about seriousness out of proportion, persistently high health anxiety, or excess time and energy on symptoms · Duration – symptomatic state persistent, typically over 6 months; any one symptom may come and go · Cause – may or may not be medically explained; a medical diagnosis does not exclude it
Defining criteria: illness anxiety disorder Fear – preoccupied with having or getting a serious illness · Symptoms – absent, or only mild · Behavior – excess health behaviors, such as body checking, or avoidance, such as of doctors and hospitals · Duration – 6 months or more
Defining criteria: functional neurological symptom disorder (conversion disorder) Symptom – 1 or more changes in voluntary motor or sensory function · Exam – findings incompatible with recognized neurologic or medical disease, such as the Hoover sign
7Treatment

Somatic symptom disorder

1

Every patientonce the diagnosis is made

Regular, brief scheduled visits

Booked on a schedule, not prompted by each new symptom.

2

Alongsideif the workup for the concern is already negative

Limit further evaluation

Unneeded tests and procedures can keep care focused on the symptom.

3

Psychotherapyscheduled visits alone are not enough

CBT (cognitive behavioral therapy)

The psychotherapy with the best evidence base. In practiceIn practice: the Merck Manual calls psychotherapy, particularly CBT, first-line; Step 2 keys regular visits with the same clinician first.

4

Medicationscheduled visits alone are not enough, especially with a coexisting psychiatric disorder

An SSRI (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor) or SNRI (serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor)

Both classes improved symptoms compared with placebo.

First treatment by situation
SituationChooseWatch for
Asks for another scan after negative workupsA scheduled brief visit; limit further testingMore testing can feed the cycle
Wants to come only when symptoms worsenVisits on a regular scheduleVisits driven by symptoms

Related disorders: first step
DisorderChoose
Illness anxiety disorderOne consistent, supportive clinician; CBT or an SSRI may help
Functional neurological symptom disorderEducation first: explain it as a real disorder shown by exam findings; CBT second line; physical therapy can help
Factitious disorderEarly psychiatric consultation; present the diagnosis without confronting or punishing; avoid risky tests and procedures
Factitious disorder imposed on anotherReport the suspicion to child protective services (adult protective services for a dependent adult)
8Follow-up
Follow-up decisions
WhenDo
Each visitKeep it regular and time-limited, on a schedule
Same concern, workup already negativeLimit further evaluation
Symptoms change, or a new symptom or objective sign appearsExamine and test it as in any patient
Throughout careWatch for suicidal threats, loss of function and harm from tests, all more common in somatic symptom disorder
Practice
  1. 38-year-old woman with 18 months of back and joint pain six specialists and normal imaging; spends hours a day researching causes has stopped working; sure something serious is missed T 36.7 °C · examination normal · blood count and inflammatory markers normal → Somatic symptom disorder → a distressing symptom with excessive thoughts and time devoted to it, persistent, typically over 6 months; illness anxiety has no or only mild symptoms, and nothing here is feigned for a reward
  2. 29-year-old man sure he has a fatal nerve disease after a friend's diagnosis no weakness; checks his grip strength many times a day worry present for 8 months examination normal · BP 122/78 mm Hg · electromyography normal → Illness anxiety disorder → preoccupation with having a serious illness for at least 6 months with no or mild symptoms and repeated body checking; somatic symptom disorder needs a distressing symptom
  3. 24-year-old woman cannot move her left leg since an argument today pushing down with the left heel when she lifts the right leg against resistance reflexes normal and symmetric · toes downgoing · brain MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) normal · T 36.8 °C → Functional neurological symptom disorder → weakness incompatible with neurologic disease: the left heel presses down when the right leg lifts (Hoover sign); normal reflexes and MRI argue against a stroke, and nothing suggests deliberate falsification
  4. 33-year-old woman, a pharmacy technician, with a thigh wound that keeps reopening cultures grow different stool organisms each time a syringe found in her bag; no lawsuit or disability claim T 38.2 °C · leukocytes 13,000/mm³ → Factitious disorder → deliberate induction of disease with deception and no obvious external reward; malingering needs an external incentive, and patients with somatic symptom disorder are not trying to deceive
  5. 45-year-old man in police custody asks for oxycodone for back pain pain started at the arrest; limps only when watched court date next week straight-leg raise negative seated and supine · strength and reflexes normal · BP 130/84 mm Hg → Malingering → symptoms overstated to obtain external incentives; factitious disorder deceives without an obvious external reward
  6. 4-year-old boy with a 2nd admission this year for blood in his urine bleeding seen only by his mother; no custody or benefit claim repeated urinalyses normal when nurses collect them T 36.9 °C · BP 96/60 mm Hg · creatinine normal → Factitious disorder imposed on another (mother) → a caregiver falsifies illness in a child without external incentives; the findings exist only in her reports and vanish under observation
  7. 36-year-old woman with abdominal pain for 3 years 11 emergency visits this year, all workups negative; fears a missed cancer asks for another computed tomography scan examination unchanged · BP 118/76 mm Hg · hemoglobin normal → Regular scheduled brief visits → regular, time-limited appointments rather than symptom-driven visits; limit further evaluation, since unnecessary testing can perpetuate symptom-focused health care use; CBT and an SSRI or SNRI can help
Pairs with Panic Disorder and Other Anxiety: is the fear about attacks, or about having a disease?
Transferable rule

Before naming a somatic symptom or related disorder, ask: is the symptom felt, feared or made on purpose, and if made, is there an external reward?
